<Rep. Mark Takano>: This legislation would pilot a three-year, $20 million-a-year grant program for community providers to receive grants of up to $1.5 million per year to deliver mental healthcare services to veterans and establish new outpatient facilities. Committee Democrats and the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) have expressed significant concerns about this bill, which would drive more resources to community providers, with fewer strings attached and even less accountability than currently exists under VA's existing Veterans Community Care Program (VCCP).
My colleagues and I fundamentally disagree with the very premise of establishing a carveout grant program for community providers of mental health, and as such could not offer any amendments that would improve this legislation. These providers already can and do furnish care to veterans through VA's existing community care authorities. A grant structure is not, in our view--or in VA's view--the right way to expand veterans' access to mental health services. At the legislative hearing on H.R. 2283, on January 13, 2026, VA cited significant concerns about this.
In addition, concerns were raised by Democratic members, by VA's witnesses, and by the minority's witness about the risk that this grant program would lead providers to ``double dip'' or even ``triple dip.'' In addition to receiving a grant, grantees could also be billing the VCCP, Medicare, and other health plans for very same care for the very same veteran. While the majority's Amendment in the Nature of a Substitute (A.N.S.) offered at the April 16, 2026, Health Subcommittee markup added a provision prohibiting such behavior, it is completely unenforceable. Because this is a grant program, without any claims submitted to VA as veterans are receiving care, there is no way for VA or this Committee to confirm providers are not double- or triple-dipping.
Furthermore, the lack of claims also gives us less oversight into the quality and safety of care delivered by grantees--we will have no claims, no returned medical records, and no insight at all into whether veterans are actually receiving evidence-based treatments. We appreciate that the majority added provisions to the A.N.S. at the full Committee markup to require grantees to be accredited and to submit ``plans'' for at least one of their providers have completed ``continuing education in the diagnosis and treatment of mental health conditions specific to veterans.'' However, a plan, for one trained provider in an entire clinic, for a $1.5 million-dollar-a-year grant, is hardly a high enough bar.
Finally, under this legislation, grantees would be able to use funds not just for direct delivery of mental healthcare. They also would be able to use funds to establish new facilities, conduct outreach, pay for clinician training, and ``support activities of the program that are not billable, reimbursable, or otherwise authorized by law.'' We would effectively be handing out $1.5 million dollars per year to community providers to use far more freely than the dollars we are sending to VA's own medical facilities.
For the reasons cited above, Committee Democrats oppose H.R. 2283, which would create a carveout grant program to funnel VA dollars to community providers of mental health, rather than investing them in VA's direct care system.
Mark Takano,
Ranking Member.
